intros.market: Five CAs control 88.78% of all certificate issuance, with Internet Security Research Group leading at 32.6%, followed by Google Trust Services at 21.0% and DigiCert at 17.8%. The top three alone hold 71.41% market share, while 74 CAs operate in the long tail with minimal issuance volume. This concentration creates both efficiency through economies of scale and systemic risk when a dominant provider experiences an incident.
intros.trust: The four major root programs collectively trust 335 roots from 88 CA organizations, but only 90 roots appear in all four stores and just 38 CA owners achieve universal inclusion. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating operational complexity where certificate chains valid in Edge may fail in other browsers. This fragmentation means CAs must navigate different trust decisions across programs, and the 245 roots trusted by fewer than four programs represent varying levels of partial trust that complicate deployment.
intros.conc: The WebPKI operates with an HHI of 2015, well above the 1500 threshold economists use to define highly concentrated markets. Three CAs issue 71.41% of all certificates, creating single points of failure where a major incident at Internet Security Research Group, Google Trust Services, or DigiCert would immediately affect nearly three-quarters of the encrypted web. This systemic dependency means the ecosystem cannot easily absorb the sudden loss of a top-tier provider, as the 74 tail CAs lack the infrastructure to rapidly scale.
intros.tail: 74 CAs operate with minimal issuance volume yet maintain full inclusion in major trust stores, creating asymmetric risk where low-revenue operators carry the same systemic trust as high-volume providers. These tail CAs collectively represent less than 12% of issuance but account for 55 of the 88 CA organizations involved in the 1697 documented incidents. The trust-versus-scale mismatch means a compliance failure at a little-used CA still compromises browsers worldwide, while the economic pressure of maintaining WebTrust/ETSI audits on thin revenue increases operational risk.
intros.geo: United States-based CAs issue 92.75% of all certificates despite representing only 15 of the 88 trusted organizations, while 44 European CAs collectively hold just 7.16% market share. Asia-Pacific hosts 17 CAs controlling 0.09% of issuance, and all CAs in the Americas outside the US and Middle East/Africa combined issue effectively zero public certificates. This geographic concentration means the WebPKI operates primarily under US corporate jurisdiction, with European regulatory frameworks like eIDAS governing only a small fraction of global issuance.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trust store inclusion but collectively issue just 0.09% of certificates, indicating their presence serves sovereign rather than commercial purposes. These CAs span the geopolitical spectrum and appear concentrated in the high-risk jurisdictions identified in the jurisdiction analysis, where state control over cryptographic infrastructure intersects with compelled disclosure laws. Their minimal issuance suggests they exist primarily for national infrastructure rather than public web services, but their root inclusion grants them technical capability to issue for any domain.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions present high compelled-disclosure risk through legal frameworks that mandate CA cooperation with state surveillance: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey represent moderate risk with developing legal authorities over cryptographic infrastructure. These classifications reflect not incident history but the structural legal power to compel CAs to issue or disclose certificates without judicial oversight, creating a threat model distinct from the operational and governance risks measured elsewhere in this observatory.
intros.ops: CAs have reported 1697 incidents across 55 organizations, with misissuance leading at 653 events, followed by 550 governance failures and 363 revocation problems. Only 30% of incidents are self-detected, while 18% come from external researchers and just 7% from audits, indicating systematic surveillance gaps that the audit intelligence analysis explores further. 225 incidents involved policy failures and 157 involved disclosure failures, showing that operational breakdowns extend beyond technical misissuance into the governance layer that root programs depend on for oversight.
intros.crypto: The cryptographic posture tab analyzes root certificate algorithms, key sizes, and standards compliance across the 335 trusted roots. SHA-1 signed roots persist in trust stores despite collision vulnerabilities, and RSA key size distribution shows some roots below current 2048-bit minimums for long-lived signing keys. The transition to post-quantum algorithms remains in early planning stages, with no production roots yet deployed using quantum-resistant signatures, creating future readiness risk as NIST finalizes PQC standards.
intros.distrust: Browsers have executed 16 formal distrust actions against CAs, with 14 of those events attributed to compliance or operational failures rather than malicious behavior. The posture distribution shows 7 cases of negligent noncompliance, 3 of demonstrated incompetence, 3 of willful circumvention, and 2 of argumentative noncompliance, with only 1 classified as purely accidental. The median runway from distrust announcement to enforcement is 1185 days, giving affected certificate holders over three years to migrate, though 10 of the 16 events involved CAs showing a pattern of repeated issues rather than isolated failures.
intros.policy: The Web PKI now imposes roughly 6657 discrete compliance obligations on CAs, a 121-fold increase since 2000, spanning CA/B Forum Baseline Requirements, four root program policies, WebTrust/ETSI audit criteria, and ISO/NIST standards. Against this expanding regulatory surface, 35 active TLS CAs show median certificate validity periods of 63 days, with only 8 ready for the 47-day maximum coming in March 2029 and 5 still issuing above the 100-day threshold that takes effect in March 2027. Three CAs remain above the 200-day limit that becomes mandatory in March 2026, demonstrating that reducing validity periods is operationally difficult even as the compliance obligations CAs must meet in shorter cycles continue to grow with zero new ballots passed since 2022 to rationalize the burden.
intros.governance: Root program oversight participation has collapsed from 67.8% Chrome and 78.0% Mozilla coverage in 2019 to just 18.4% and 9.9% respectively in 2025, with Apple dropping to 5.4% and Microsoft at 0.0%. Chrome and Mozilla have commented on 738 and 820 total incident bugs but substantively engaged on only 296 and 250, with recent substantive participation falling to 115 and 48 respectively. This declining oversight occurs even as the 1697 incidents documented across 55 CAs create an expanding workload, leaving CAs increasingly self-supervised despite the governance failures representing 550 of those incidents.
intros.community: The CA/Browser Forum has 56 members, but only 21 actively participate in ballot work, leaving 35 organizations with zero contribution to the standards they must implement. Sectigo leads organizational participation, while Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots and endorsed 1, demonstrating concentrated leadership where a few individuals drive policy for an ecosystem serving billions of users. This silent majority pattern means the regulatory surface described in the BR readiness analysis expands through decisions made by a small active minority rather than broad consensus among the CAs bearing compliance costs.
intros.audit: Auditors detected just 28% of the 429 in-scope incidents that occurred during their audit periods, meaning 310 compliance failures produced clean opinions. 42 CAs show high transparency gaps between their audit letters and their Bugzilla incident history, while only 5 audits resulted in qualified opinions despite the documented failure rate. 79 parsed WebTrust letters show 62.5% self-report incidents, and 32 ETSI audits show 69.1% self-reporting, indicating that most audit findings come from CA disclosure rather than auditor detection. The auditor market shows an HHI of 553.2 across the top firms, with KPMG covering 11 CAs at 76.4% average quality but 99.6 day average transparency gap, demonstrating that even high-quality audit processes operate on delayed information that misses real-time operational failures.
